summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Within this national framework, the North West carries a specific and severe care gap. MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023 that trans residents of the province cannot obtain hormone replacement therapy at any public health facility there, and that people travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to receive it. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission. A trans visitor dependent on prescribed HRT should expect to arrive with a supply sufficient for the stay or to plan cross-province travel for refills.

A parallel customary-law jurisdiction is a further exposure. HRW reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. HRW also reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Visitors to rural areas of the North West, which contains former Bantustan territory, come within reach of that machinery.

Institutional enforcement of gender norms extends to schools. MambaOnline reported on 23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News, that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt since she was a girl, and she missed three weeks of classes. The case records a North West institution applying a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil in a province with a socially conservative enforcement climate.

Research coverage of the province is thin. A report titled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010 from a survey conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella, questioned 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces about openness about same-sex sexuality, perceptions of their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
South Africa's evidence base on anti-LGBT hate crimes is unusually small for a country with this level of statutory protection. Love Not Hate campaign research conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being and published in 2016 found only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people in the country: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 study of North West province, and the campaign's own national study measuring levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally. The 2010 North West survey remains one of the very few province-level measurements anywhere in the country.

Comparison with neighbouring provinces sharpens the care gap. Public hormone replacement therapy is available in Gauteng, which is why North West residents journey to Soweto; the absence is provincial, not national. The same pattern of unequal access appears elsewhere in the country, with the East London memorandum to Frere Hospital documenting year-long delays in a different province.

The North West is described in the 2010 survey as one of South Africa's poorest and most under-populated provinces, and its population is largely rural. Sparse settlement and thin service coverage plausibly compound both the health-care absence and the isolation of LGBT people from police cooperation and formal courts, though the sources do not measure that causal link directly.

The customary-law route is not a South African norm but a contested proposal. HRW's 2012 objections concerned a bill before parliament that would have extended chiefs' courts with no opt-out; whether the customary fora HRW describes were themselves established under that bill or under pre-existing authority is not settled by the sources here.
localsOnly:
Provincial residents carrying a prescription for hormone replacement therapy have no public facility in the North West able to fill it, and the North West Department of Health acknowledged this in its reply to the complaint Action for Social Justice International lodged with the South African Human Rights Commission. Continuity of treatment depends on travel to Gauteng or on private supply.

Rural residents and those in former Bantustan areas may be drawn into chiefs' courts, which HRW reported punish lesbians in rural areas, alongside a police relationship that HRW characterised as poor cooperation. Formal constitutional remedies sit alongside, rather than in place of, that parallel system.

School pupils in the province face institutional gender policing of dress, as the 2016 barring of Zinzi Manini Molema from Maphoitsile village for refusing a skirt illustrates. The 2010 provincial survey targeted exactly this population: 319 LGBT people, largely rural, reporting on openness, perceived environment, sexual abuse and discrimination.

Legal gender recognition nationally still runs through medical evidence and a binary classification, and the 2024 Gender Dynamix documentation of police mockery when a trans woman sought to file a domestic-violence complaint indicates the risk attached to presenting identity documents that do not match presentation. Protests about the resulting humiliation and denial of service are directed at national legislation rather than provincial administration.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Traditional Courts Bill is unresolved here. The inventory records HRW's objections as of 29 May 2012 and describes the customary fora HRW said already punished lesbians in rural areas, but it does not state whether the bill was subsequently enacted, amended or withdrawn, nor whether the customary courts HRW described predate it. The scope of customary jurisdiction in the North West as of 2025 is therefore not sourced.

Whether any North West facility began providing hormone replacement therapy after the February 2023 report is unresolved. The most recent sourced statement is the North West Department of Health's confirmation that it had none at the time of its reply to the SAHRC complaint; no later inventory item updates it.

The outcome of the 2016 school case is not sourced. The report establishes the three-week exclusion of the pupil and the principal's stated reason, but records no finding by a department, equality court or other body.

Implementation of the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for transgender inmates is unverified. The August 2025 reporting in the parent framework records doubt from rights organisations, and no source here measures compliance after the November 2025 orders. Whether the orders have been carried out remains unresolved.

No source in this inventory records a North West–specific hate-crime figure for trans people. The 2010 provincial survey is dated and its published findings are not reproduced here, and the national counts cited (five LGBTQIA+ murders in December 2024) are not broken down by province.
